title: Token reservoir & latency-hysteresis routing playbook for dedicated→hosted overflow
creator: Priya Kaur
description:
Problem: During regional traffic spikes we often see oscillation between Dedicated capacity (tenant-owned GPU pools) and Hosted backfill when short bursts exceed committed throughput. Existing guardrails either (a) immediately spill to hosted which raises cost and potential QoS differences, or (b) hard-reserve tokens which underutilizes Dedicated.

This ticket proposes a playbook and implementation sketch for a token-reservoir based routing policy combined with latency-hysteresis to: (1) allow short, predictable bursts on Dedicated without immediate spill to Hosted, (2) prevent oscillatory thrashing between Dedicated and Hosted, and (3) provide clear telemetry/headers for downstream services to make cost/quality tradeoffs.

Core idea: allocate a replenishing per-tenant "token reservoir" on Dedicated. Each request consumes tokens proportional to expected cost (tokens ~= estimated compute/time/window). When reservoir is depleted, requests are routed to Hosted. A latency-hysteresis controller monitors p50/p95 latency and prevents reservoirs from being refilled aggressively if Dedicated latency degrades, thereby implementing graceful demotion. The system emits explicit signals (X-Reservoir-State, X-Reservoir-TTL, routing_decision_reason) so Console and SDKs can expose why a request hit Hosted.
acceptance_criteria: Define token accounting schema (token cost per model variant + multiplier for sequence length) documented in Confluence
Prototype router implements per-tenant reservoir with replenish-rate and max-capacity configs
Latency-hysteresis controller observes p50/p95 and enforces refill backoff when p95 > configured SLO margin
System emits routing signals in headers and telemetry; Console shows per-tenant reservoir burn and refill rates
End-to-end tests: synthetic burst traffic causes short drain+refill without immediate spill, and sustained overload drains reservoir and falls back to Hosted
Runbook updated with playbook for manual interventions and rollback steps
design_notes:
Token accounting: base tokens = model_cost_table[model_variant] * (seq_len / 512). Reservoir config: {capacity_tokens, replenish_tokens_per_sec, min_reservoir_fraction}. Refill backoff: linear decay with exponential factor if p95 remains above SLO for >30s.

Routing decision order (fast path): 1) Check soft reservations for tenant (hard reservations still respected) 2) If reservoir.tokens >= request.token_cost -> route to Dedicated and decrement 3) Else consult fallback policy: use Hosted if allowed by tenant tier OR try queued short-delay (50-200ms) to wait for replenish 4) Emit routing_decision_reason: [DEDICATED_OK | DEDICATED_DEPLETED | HYSTERESIS_BLOCK | QUEUED_RETRY]
implementation_tasks: Add reservoir metadata to tenant config and admin API (console + infra) (ENG backend + config-schema)
Implement in edge router: in-memory token cache + consistent hashing for reservoir ownership
Integrate latency-hysteresis controller tied to existing SLO metrics (p50/p95) in metrics pipeline
Add SDK/REST header propagation (X-Reservoir-State, X-Reservoir-Remaining, routing_decision_reason)
Telemetry: new Grafana panels and Console widgets for reservoir burn, refill_rate, triggered_hysteresis_events
E2E tests: load generator scenarios (burst 10x for 30s, sustained 3x) and validate routing outcomes
Create a canary rollout plan: start with low-risk tenants (internal staging customers)
tradeoffs_and_decisions:
Tradeoffs: a reservoir increases Dedicated utilization and behavioral predictability at the cost of implementation complexity and slightly delayed fallback when necessary. To reduce cost risk, reservoirs will be smaller for non-enterprise tiers and will include tenant-configurable caps.

Quality vs cost: some requests will run on Hosted during sustained overload which may have different quantization/latency. We will surface explicit reasons and token costs so product teams can choose model variants or degrade gracefully.

Decision: Prefer soft reservoirs + hysteresis over aggressive immediate spill to Hosted to avoid stateful thrash and to preserve SLOs for non-burst traffic. If p95 latency degrades >15% vs baseline for >30s, we enter HYSTERESIS mode which prevents refills until stable for 2x the degradation window.

runbook_notes: If Dedicated latency p95 crosses Service SLO and hysteresis engaged, Console shows 'Reservoir: HYSTERESIS' and auto-routes to Hosted after queued retries fail
Manual override: admin API to force-drain or freeze reservoirs for tenant (useful during incidents)
Rollback: disable reservoir feature flag and revert router config; flush in-memory counters and restart shards
Incident indicators: reservoir_burn_rate >> replenish_rate for >2 minutes; rising queued_retries and increased hosted_fallback_rate
examples: Scenario A (short burst): tenant with capacity_capacity=100rps and reservoir_capacity_tokens=50k receives 200rps for 20s. Router consumes reservoir tokens and maintains Dedicated routing with small latency impact; reservoir refills over next 5 minutes.

Scenario B (sustained overload): same tenant receives 200rps for 10min. Reservoir depletes in ~1min; hysteresis observes p95 > SLO at 80s and blocks refills; remaining requests route to Hosted until baseline returns. Post-incident, replenish backoff prevents immediate thrash.
risks_and_mitigations: Risk: Token misaccounting due to clock skew -> Mitigation: short-lease decrement + periodic reconciliation and counters persisted to RocksDB for shard restarts
Risk: Complexity increases debugging surface -> Mitigation: Clear headers + Console displays + linkable trace IDs for reservoir events
Risk: Cost leak if reservoirs too permissive -> Mitigation: per-tenant caps, tier-based defaults, and monthly cost alerts
